t: The space station sees 16 sunrises a day
b: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up at roughly 28,000 km/h. It circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

q.p: How many sunrises do ISS astronauts see each day?

rq.p: How long does one ISS orbit take?

why: 24 hours ÷ 90 minutes ≈ 16 orbits.

b: Without gravity squashing the spine, the discs between vertebrae spread out. Astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller in orbit, often a few centimetres. They shrink back within months of returning to Earth.

q.p: What happens to astronauts' height in space?

rq.p: Why do astronauts grow in orbit?

why: Gravity normally compresses your spine slightly every day.
src: Effect of spaceflight on the human body

b: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month, roughly two to three times faster than toenails. A whole fingernail regrows in around six months; a big toenail can take over a year.

q.p: Which grow faster?

rq.p: How long does a fingernail take to fully regrow?

why: Nail growth links to blood flow and use, both higher in fingers.

t: Giraffes have seven neck bones, like you
b: Despite their huge necks, giraffes have the same number of neck vertebrae as humans and most mammals: seven. Each giraffe neck bone can be over 25 cm long.

q.p: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?

rq.p: How does a giraffe's neck get so long?
o: Each of the seven bones is very long

why: Almost all mammals share the seven-vertebra plan.

b: Adult elephants can't jump. Their bones point straight down to support their weight, and their ankles lack the springiness needed. Even when moving fast, an elephant keeps at least one foot on the ground.

q.p: Can an adult elephant jump?

rq.p: When moving fast, an elephant always keeps…

why: Pillar-like legs suit carrying weight, not springing.

b: Big cats split into two groups. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars can roar thanks to a stretchy throat structure. Cheetahs have a rigid one, like house cats, so they purr, chirp and meow instead.

q.p: Which sound can a cheetah make?

rq.p: What lets lions roar but not cheetahs?

why: The roaring cats have a flexible, partly ossified hyoid.

t: Flamingos are pink because of food
b: Flamingos aren't born pink. Their colour comes from pigments called carotenoids in the algae and tiny shrimp they eat. Flamingos in zoos are fed supplements, or they fade toward white.

q.p: Why are flamingos pink?

rq.p: What colour are flamingo chicks?

why: Carotenoids are the same pigments that make carrots orange.

t: Starfish have no brain and no blood
b: Sea stars have no brain, instead using a ring of nerves around their mouth. They also have no blood: they pump seawater through a network of canals to move their tiny tube feet.

q.p: What does a starfish lack?

rq.p: What do sea stars pump through their bodies?

why: The water vascular system replaces blood for movement.

t: A jellyfish that can turn back time
b: When stressed or injured, the 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii can turn its adult body back into a young polyp and start its life cycle again. It can still be eaten or get sick, but it can, in theory, avoid dying of old age.

q.p: What can the 'immortal jellyfish' do?
o: Regrow from one cell in a day

rq.p: Can the immortal jellyfish still die?

why: Its cells can transform into other cell types.

b: Peacock mantis shrimp swing a club-like limb at about 80 km/h, with acceleration similar to a small-calibre bullet. The strike is so fast it creates bubbles that collapse with a second blow of heat and light. They smash crab shells open.

q.p: What's special about a mantis shrimp's strike?
o: One of the fastest punches in nature

rq.p: What extra force does the strike create?
o: A sound wave that stuns fish

why: The limb is spring-loaded and released like a catapult.

b: A honeybee that finds food returns to the hive and performs a 'waggle dance'. The angle of the dance relative to straight up tells others the direction relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle tells the distance.

q.p: How do honeybees tell each other where food is?

rq.p: In the waggle dance, what does waggle length show?

why: Karl von Frisch decoded the dance and won a Nobel Prize in 1973.

b: An owl's eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets, so it can't roll them. Instead it can rotate its head up to about 270 degrees. Extra neck vertebrae and special blood vessels keep blood flowing while it twists.

q.p: Why do owls turn their heads so far?

rq.p: About how far can an owl turn its head?

why: Owl eyes are tubular, giving big pupils but no movement.

b: In 2019 scientists described a new electric eel species, Electrophorus voltai, which can discharge up to 860 volts, the strongest known from any animal. A UK mains socket supplies 230 volts. Electric eels are actually knifefish, not true eels.

q.p: What's the strongest shock recorded from an animal?

rq.p: What are electric eels, really?

why: Thousands of special cells stack up like batteries.

t: Some bamboo grows nearly a metre a day
b: Certain bamboo species can grow up to about 90 cm in a single day, among the fastest growth of any plant. Bamboo is technically a giant grass, and a new shoot can reach full height in just a few months.

q.p: Bamboo is a type of…

rq.p: How fast can some bamboo grow?
o: Up to about 90 cm a day

why: Each segment stretches at once rather than growing from the tip.

t: The smell of rain has a name
b: That earthy smell after rain is called petrichor. Much of it comes from geosmin, a chemical made by soil bacteria. Human noses are extraordinarily sensitive to geosmin, detecting it at concentrations of just a few parts per trillion.

q.p: What makes the earthy smell after rain?

rq.p: What is the smell after rain called?

why: Raindrops kick geosmin and plant oils into the air.

t: Magnetic north is on the move
b: The north magnetic pole, where compasses point, wanders as Earth's molten iron core churns. In the early 2000s it was drifting about 50 km a year, from Canada toward Siberia. Maps and phone navigation are updated to keep up.

q.p: Does magnetic north stay in one place?

rq.p: What makes the magnetic pole move?
o: Churning liquid iron in Earth's core

why: Earth's magnetic field comes from flowing metal deep inside.

b: Rocks record that Earth's magnetic north and south have swapped many times. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago. Reversals take hundreds to thousands of years and don't follow a regular schedule.

q.p: Have Earth's magnetic poles ever swapped?

rq.p: When was the last full magnetic reversal?

why: Magnetic minerals in cooling lava lock in the field's direction.

t: Seasons come from tilt, not distance
b: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter. Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, so each hemisphere takes turns getting more direct sunlight and longer days.

q.p: Why is it warmer in summer?
o: Earth's tilt gives more direct sunlight
Earth is closer to the Sun

rq.p: When is Earth closest to the Sun?

why: Direct light concentrates more energy on each patch of ground.

b: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded thousands of moonquakes. Some come from deep inside, some from meteorite hits, and some from the surface warming after the long lunar night. Shallow moonquakes can rumble on for many minutes.

q.p: Does the Moon have earthquakes?

rq.p: How do we know about moonquakes?

why: Earth's tides stretch the Moon, and its surface expands and contracts with heat.

t: The 'dark side' of the Moon isn't dark
b: The Moon always shows us the same face, so the other half is called the far side. It gets just as much sunlight as the near side. During a new Moon, when we see no light, the far side is fully lit.

q.p: Does the far side of the Moon get sunlight?
o: Yes, as much as the near side

rq.p: Why do we only see one side of the Moon?

why: 'Dark' meant unknown, not unlit.

b: A shooting star, or meteor, is usually a speck of space dust no bigger than a grain of sand. It hits the atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second and burns up about 100 km above the ground, glowing as it goes.

q.p: How big is a typical shooting star?

rq.p: Why do meteors glow?
o: They heat up hitting the air at huge speed

why: Speed, not size, makes the light show.

b: On a dark night, the Andromeda Galaxy is a faint smudge visible without a telescope. It's about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light reaching your eye left when early human ancestors walked Earth.

q.p: What's the most distant thing you can see without a telescope?

rq.p: How long ago did Andromeda's light leave it?

why: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.

b: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air, but around 1,480 metres per second in water, roughly four times faster. Water molecules are packed closer, so vibrations pass along more quickly.

q.p: Where does sound travel faster?

rq.p: About how much faster is sound in water than air?

why: Denser, stiffer materials carry vibrations faster.

b: 'Blind as a bat' is a myth. All bats can see, and many fruit bats have excellent eyesight and don't echolocate at all. Echolocating bats use both their eyes and their ears.

q.p: Are bats blind?

rq.p: Which bats often rely mostly on eyesight?

why: Echolocation adds to vision; it doesn't replace it.

b: Emperor penguins are the deepest-diving birds. They've been recorded diving more than 500 metres and holding their breath for over 20 minutes while hunting fish and squid.

q.p: Which bird dives the deepest?

rq.p: How long can emperor penguins hold their breath?

why: They slow their heart and store oxygen in muscles.
